action_criteria.expected_evidence: Solitary right frontotemporal lesion with a thin, relatively smooth ring and a medial nodular component, central restricted diffusion, extensive oedema and 4 mm midline shift
action_criteria.label: Order MRI brain with and without gadolinium (tumour protocol with DWI, FLAIR, post-contrast T1) to characterise the right frontotemporal lesion, define mass effect and plan surgery
action_criteria.rationale: Contrast-enhanced MRI with diffusion and FLAIR is the standard imaging for a suspected diffuse glioma: it defines the enhancing target, the oedema and the mass effect, and plans the surgical approach (EANO 2021).

action_criteria.expected_evidence: rCBV 2.8 in the enhancing rim and low in the core, favouring tumour over abscess
action_criteria.label: Order MR perfusion (DSC) to assess tumour vascularity and target the most aggressive region for tissue sampling
action_criteria.rationale: Elevated rCBV supports a high-grade neoplasm and identifies the region to sample; it does not grade or exclude, tissue decides (Law 2003). An abscess rim usually has low rCBV.

action_criteria.expected_evidence: Rim choline elevation with no amino-acid, acetate or succinate peaks, favouring tumour over pyogenic abscess
action_criteria.label: Order MR spectroscopy (1H-MRS) to characterise the metabolic profile of the lesion
action_criteria.rationale: Elevated choline with reduced NAA and lipid-lactate supports a high-grade neoplasm; it does not establish the diagnosis, tissue does (Bulik 2013).

action_criteria.expected_evidence: No extracranial primary or systemic metastatic disease in a former smoker
action_criteria.label: Order CT chest, abdomen and pelvis with contrast if a solitary metastasis remains on the differential
action_criteria.rationale: Staging for an extracranial primary is optional when the imaging favours a primary glioma and there is no history of cancer.

action_criteria.label: Draw two sets of blood cultures because a pyogenic brain abscess remains possible
action_criteria.rationale: An odontogenic brain abscess is on the differential; blood cultures can identify the organism before aspiration and guide antibiotic choice.

action_criteria.expected_evidence: Sterile aspirate with no organisms and integrated diagnosis Glioblastoma, IDH-wildtype, CNS WHO grade 4, with wildtype IDH1/IDH2 under age 55, retained ATRX and unmethylated MGMT
action_criteria.label: Obtain tissue by stereotactic aspiration and biopsy of the right frontotemporal lesion with frozen section, Gram stain and culture, or by resection, for an integrated histomolecular diagnosis with IDH1 R132H immunohistochemistry, IDH1/IDH2 sequencing, ATRX immunohistochemistry and MGMT promoter methylation
action_criteria.rationale: Aspiration comes first because abscess remains possible and aspiration is diagnostic and therapeutic; frozen section, Gram stain and culture separate abscess from necrotic tumour. Only tissue establishes the integrated diagnosis and the molecular results that select treatment (EANO 2021); under age 55 IDH sequencing is needed after negative IDH1 R132H immunohistochemistry.

prohibited_recommendations: Do not perform a lumbar puncture: the right frontotemporal mass causes a 4 mm midline shift with subfalcine herniation, and the pressure gradient risks herniation.
Do not start radiotherapy, temozolomide or other tumour-directed therapy before the integrated tissue diagnosis is established.
Do not start therapeutic anticoagulation without a clear thromboembolic indication, given the planned neurosurgery and bleeding risk.
Do not use enzyme-inducing antiseizure drugs (phenytoin, carbamazepine, phenobarbital), which interact with dexamethasone and temozolomide.
required_recommendations: Refer urgently to neurosurgery for stereotactic aspiration and biopsy of the right frontotemporal lesion with frozen section, Gram stain and aerobic, anaerobic and fungal culture, proceeding to resection when tumour is confirmed; send the tissue for an integrated histomolecular diagnosis (WHO CNS5) including IDH, ATRX and MGMT.

Ask infectious diseases to review before surgery because an odontogenic abscess is possible; if the patient is stable and aspiration is within hours, take the aspirate before empirical antibiotics, and start them at once if he deteriorates or surgery is delayed (ESCMID 2024: antimicrobials may be withheld until aspiration in patients without severe disease when neurosurgery is possible within about 24 hours).
Arrange dental review of the right lower second molar extraction site to exclude a residual odontogenic source.

Start dexamethasone for symptomatic vasogenic oedema (for example 4 mg every 6 to 8 hours after a loading dose when mass effect is marked) at the lowest effective dose, with glucose monitoring and gastric protection, and taper after surgery.

Start antiseizure treatment with levetiracetam for the generalized tonic-clonic seizure, with the staring spells of the past week; this is treatment of tumour-related epilepsy, not prophylaxis. Avoid enzyme-inducing antiseizure drugs (phenytoin, carbamazepine, phenobarbital), which lower dexamethasone and chemotherapy exposure.
Monitor capillary glucose during dexamethasone in this patient with type 2 diabetes on metformin, and adjust the antihyperglycaemic regimen, with insulin if needed.
Stop as-needed ibuprofen before neurosurgery and while on dexamethasone (platelet inhibition and gastrointestinal bleeding risk); use paracetamol for headache.

After the integrated diagnosis, refer to the neuro-oncology multidisciplinary team; for glioblastoma, IDH-wildtype, at age 48 with KPS 80, the standard is radiotherapy 60 Gy in 30 fractions with concomitant and adjuvant temozolomide (Stupp 2005; EANO 2021); with an unmethylated MGMT promoter the benefit of temozolomide is smaller, so clinical trial options should also be discussed.

patient.history_present_illness: This 48-year-old right-handed man was brought to the emergency department by ambulance after a witnessed generalized tonic-clonic seizure at home. He has no prior history of seizures. According to his wife, the patient has been experiencing progressive headaches over the past three weeks, which he initially attributed to the stress associated with a recent dental abscess and subsequent treatment. The headaches were described as diffuse, worse in the morning upon awakening, and occasionally accompanied by mild nausea. Over-the-counter ibuprofen provided only partial relief. Approximately three weeks prior to this presentation, he was treated for a dental abscess of his right lower second molar with incision and drainage, and was prescribed a 14-day course of amoxicillin-clavulanate, which he completed one week ago. His dentist noted the abscess had been present for at least several days before he sought care, and there was concern about the severity of the infection at the time of drainage. The patient's wife reports that over the past two weeks she has noticed subtle personality changes: he has become more irritable than usual, has been less engaged with the family, and twice forgot to pick up their daughter from soccer practice, which she describes as completely out of character. He also had difficulty preparing a lesson plan for his class last week and needed to ask a colleague for help, which he has never done before. The patient himself downplays these symptoms, attributing them to fatigue and lingering discomfort from the dental procedure. He denies any focal weakness, numbness, visual changes, or difficulty with speech. He denies fever, chills, night sweats, or weight loss. The seizure occurred this morning while he was eating breakfast. His wife witnessed tonic stiffening followed by clonic jerking of all four extremities lasting approximately 90 seconds. He was postictal and confused for approximately 15 minutes afterward. Upon arrival to the emergency department, a non-contrast CT of the head was performed and showed a hypodense lesion in the right frontotemporal region with surrounding oedema and mild mass effect.

neurological_exam.additional: Examination performed 2 hours after the generalized tonic-clonic seizure at home, once the post-ictal confusion had resolved; it was essentially non-focal. His wife reports that for the past week he has been intermittently 'staring off' for 5 to 10 seconds at a time, which the family attributed to fatigue or stress.
